name: APT26
affiliation_detail:
Attributed to the Jiangsu Bureau of the Ministry of State Security (JSSD, 江苏省国家安全厅), the provincial MSS office in Nanjing.
U.S. DOJ indicements did not specifically name APT26. CrowdStrike's October 2019 report synthesized multiple DOJ indictments (August 2017 – October 2018) into a single picture, demonstrating that the JSSD coordinated both cyber intrusions (Turbine Panda) and traditional recruitment of insiders at targeted aerospace firms, under unified bureau direction.
Two JSSD officers named in the Zhang et al. indictment — Chai Meng (cyber operations director) and Liu Chunliang (infrastructure manager) — allegedly oversaw the cyber component. JSSD intelligence officer Xu Yanjun, according to the indictment, directed recruitment of insiders.
description:
APT26 / Turbine Panda is a Chinese state-sponsored cyber espionage group, per U.S. DOJ indictment operated by the Jiangsu State Security Department (JSSD), a provincial bureau of the Ministry of State Security headquartered in Nanjing.
The group is most notable for its role in the theft of aerospace intellectual property supporting the COMAC C919 passenger jet development, running from approximately 2010 to 2015.
Integration between cyber operations and HUMINT was noted by a series of DOJ indicements and CrowdStrike reporting. CrowdStrike 2019 report states that the JSSD assigned one officer (Chai Meng) to direct the cyber team and another (Xu Yanjun) to recruit ethnic Chinese insiders at target firms. When the hackers could not penetrate a target network remotely, insiders were used to deliver malware Sakula (used exclusively in APT26-associated campaigns) via USB drives. 
MSS officer Xu Yanjun was arrested in Belgium in 2018 and later sentenced to 20 years in prison. In 2024, Xu was sent to China in prisoners swap deal. Insiders Zheng Xiaoqing and Ji Chaoqun, were both sentenced, to 24 months and 8 years respectively. (DOJ, 2023; BBC, 2023)  Sakula developer Yu Pingan was arrested in 2017 in Los Angeles and charged. (BBC, 2017)
JSSD was also linked to the 2015 OPM breach (22 million personnel records) and the Anthem breach (80 million health records) through shared use of the Sakula RAT and overlapping infrastructure and TTPs. These connections are CrowdStrike's (2019) analytical assessment and have not been confirmed by DOJ indictment.
APT26 does not have a dedicated MITRE ATT&CK group entry.

campaigns.name: COMAC C919 Supply Chain Espionage
campaigns.description: Systematic targeting of Western aerospace suppliers to the COMAC C919 passenger jet. JSSD coordinated cyber intrusions by Turbine Panda with HUMINT recruitment of insiders at target firms. Victims included GE Aviation, Safran, Honeywell, Ametek, and Capstone Turbine. Malware deployed included Sakula, PlugX, and Winnti. Insiders planted Sakula via USB when remote access failed. In 2016, AECC unveiled the CJ-1000AX engine, which closely resembled the CFM LEAP-1C/LEAP-X engines produced by the targeted firms. CrowdStrike assessed the campaign allowed COMAC to trim "several years and potentially billions of dollars" off development time.

campaigns.name: OPM / Anthem Breaches (assessed)
campaigns.description: CrowdStrike assessed that the JSSD was behind the 2015 OPM breach (22+ million federal personnel records) and the Anthem breach (~80 million health records). The assessment is based on: (1) shared Sakula malware usage between these breaches and confirmed Turbine Panda operations; (2) similar TTPs between the Anthem intrusion and a prior Ametek breach attributed to Turbine Panda; (3) IsSpace malware used in both the Anthem/OPM intrusions and the C919 campaign. This attribution has not been confirmed by DOJ indictment and remains an analytical assessment. Other vendors have used the Deep Panda designation for this activity.
